1	# /acs:analyze-requirements — the survey: mode, inputs and the previous analysis
2	
3	Open this before the `plan` action: how the run's mode and folders are
4	derived, what the context fields and the keys `acs.py artifacts show` prints
5	mean for this run, which inputs every survey lane is named, and what each
6	lane records, down to the four groups of questions the survey ends with.
7	
8	**Where the cross-references below point.** "Two modes", "Stage 1",
9	"Stage 2" and "Stage 3" are SKILL.md's sections; "The feature" is
10	`references/clarify.md`.
11	
12	## The mode and the folders
13	
14	A Development run **starts from the feature's living analysis** when one
15	exists: it is a Stage 1 reuse input, exactly like a previous analysis of the
16	same run (Inputs, item 7) — the survey re-verifies it against the current code
17	and narrows it to this change; it is never copied and never edited by this run.
18	`<prd_dir>` and `<development_dir>` are found deterministically
19	(`acs_lib.requirements.prd_dir` / `development_dir`: a settings key, then the
20	docs the repo already has, defaulting to `docs/product` and
21	`docs/development`) — you never guess them, and `acs.py artifacts show` and
22	`acs.py analysis publish` print the resolved paths. The mode is derived, never
23	chosen by you (`context.requirements.phase`); only when the user explicitly
24	asks for the feature's living analysis on a run that would be Development
25	(e.g. "analyze the wishlist feature as a whole", naming a ticket for context)
26	record it — `acs.py analysis plan --mode discovery` when you declare the
27	lanes, or `{"phase": "discovery"}` with `acs.py requirements refine`.
28	
29	## The context fields, in full
30	
31	`--args` is the invocation's raw argument text — the ticket id, document paths
32	and prompt, in any order and any mix. `step start` parses it into the run's
33	sources (a `<PREFIX>-<n>` token is a ticket, a token naming an existing file is
34	a document, everything else is the prompt), copies a document from outside
35	the repo into the run and hashes it, and writes the run's `requirements.md`;
36	on a host whose Skill pre-hook already did this it is idempotent.
37	
38	In `context.requirements`, `path` is the run's
39	`requirements.md` — the ticket's title, description and acceptance criteria
40	numbered `AC-1…`, the prompt verbatim, each document inlined (markdown,
41	text) or cited by its run copy under `<run>/subject/` (a PDF or an image:
42	Read that copy), and a `## Refined` section only `acs.py requirements
43	refine` writes. `sources` lists the containers (`ticket` / `document` /
44	`prompt`); `feature` is the feature this analysis is filed under once one is
45	known (refined, else the ticket's first `features` slug); `phase` is the
46	mode — `development` when the run has a ticket or `/acs:ship` drives it,
47	else `discovery` (Two modes, above); `feature_analysis` is the feature's
48	living analysis when one exists. A later invocation that
49	names new containers adds them (`acs.py requirements add --args "…"`), and
50	`requirements.md` is regenerated, never edited by hand.
51	
52	- `design` — `{exists, dir, source}`: the tech design found for the run —
53	  its own (`source` `"own"`), else its parent epic's (`"parent"`). `design.dir`
54	  is the folder the found file is in. When `design.exists`, read
55	  `tech-design.md` there (a legacy `design.md` when no `tech-design.md`
56	  exists). Call it `<design_doc>`; the
57	  analysis is bounded by a design that already exists, never a second opinion
58	  on it. With none, analyze without one and say nothing about design.
59	
60	## Resolving the previous analysis
61	
62	- `artifacts["analysis.md"]` non-null → the existing analysis: the folder's
63	  `README.md` (the key keeps its old name), with every file of the folder in
64	  `analysis_files`, README first. It is the PREVIOUS analysis of this subject
65	  (on a Discovery run, the feature's living analysis itself). Stage 1's survey
66	  starts from it (reuse — see Stage 1), and this run REVISES it in place (a
67	  re-analysis after new information, never a second folder). Call it
68	  `<previous_analysis>`.
69	- `paths["analysis.md"]` non-null → where this run publishes: the target
70	  folder's `README.md` (the feature root on a Discovery run, `docs_dir` — the
71	  Development folder — otherwise). It is null until the run has a feature.
72	- no checkout to anchor the docs folder to → the analysis is published to the
73	  run partition's `analysis/` — the partition fallback, for the no-checkout
74	  case only.
75	
76	On a Development run, `feature_analysis` names the feature's living analysis
77	(`<prd_dir>/features/<feature>/analysis/README.md`) when it exists: a second
78	reuse input, read and never written. Call it `<feature_analysis>`.
79	
80	A run with no feature yet cannot resolve a previous analysis. When the
81	invocation itself names the feature — the prompt says which ("the order
82	tracking feature"), or a PRD feature document is among the sources — that is
83	the user's answer already: record it in the ledger and with `acs.py
84	requirements refine` (`{"feature": "<slug>"}`, Stage 2's "The feature"), then
85	resolve again, BEFORE the survey, so it starts from the feature's living
86	analysis. Otherwise the requirements lane reads the living analysis of each
87	candidate feature it proposes (`<prd_dir>/features/<slug>/analysis/README.md`,
88	when present).
89	
90	A legacy `docs/tickets/<id>/analysis.md` from before ADR-0128 is still READ
91	(it is the previous analysis when the new folder has none), and so is a
92	legacy single-file `analysis.md` in the phase folder from before ADR-0133;
93	nothing writes either any more — the revision is published as a folder to
94	`paths["analysis.md"]`. This is exactly what `acs_lib.artifacts.artifact_path`
95	resolves, what `acs.py analysis publish` writes to, and what the next skills
96	read through `acs.py artifacts show`, so the path this run publishes is the
97	path they find. A run with no feature yet has no folder to
98	publish to: `publish` refuses until Stage 2 records one.
99	
100	## The inputs, in order
101	
102	1. The requirements — `requirements.md` at `context.requirements.path`, and
103	   every document copy it cites (a PDF or an image under `<run>/subject/`,
104	   which the lanes Read themselves): the ticket's title, description and
105	   acceptance criteria, the prompt, the documents, in that order. When the
106	   run has a ticket, also its file (whatever `acs.py artifacts show` reports
107	   as `source_path`) for its type and parent.
108	2. `<design_doc>` when `design.exists` — the decided architecture.
109	   The analysis maps the requirements onto that decision; it never re-opens it.
110	3. The PRD and the living requirements set when they exist — what the
111	   product already promises about this area, and the feature list the
112	   feature slug is chosen from (`<prd_dir>/prd.md`, whose Features index links
113	   each feature's own PRD — its requirements `R<n>` and acceptance criteria — and
114	   the feature folders under `<prd_dir>/features/`). Locate them, and the architecture set below, the
115	   way any session finds a document: CLAUDE.md and whatever docs index it or
116	   the repo points at (e.g. `docs/README.md`), then a Glob/Grep by file name
117	   or content (`prd.md`, a `requirements/` folder, `hld/tech-stack.md`;
118	   conventionally under `docs/product/`, `docs/requirements/`,
119	   `docs/architecture/`). Not found → not an input.
120	4. The architecture doc set when it exists (`hld/`, `lld/flows/`,
121	   `lld/contracts.md`) — the components the impact map names are the
122	   components those docs name, and the code areas you declare (the `plan` action) are
123	   the components they separate.
124	5. The consumer repo itself: the source, tests, docs and configuration the
125	   requirements touch. The impact map is derived from the CODE, not from the
126	   requirements' prose.
127	6. The clarification ledger (`clarify.py list`, `--ticket <id>` on a ticket
128	   run; a ticketless run's ledger is the run's own) — answers already
129	   recorded are inputs, not questions to ask again.
130	7. `<previous_analysis>` when `artifacts["analysis.md"]` exists — the last
131	   published analysis of this subject, its README and every file in
132	   `analysis_files` — and, on a Development run,
133	   `<feature_analysis>`, the feature's living analysis. The survey starts from
134	   them rather than from nothing, and re-verifies them against the current
135	   code (Stage 1).
136	
137	## What the survey records
138	
139	The `survey` action. The requirements lane (`phase="analyst"`
140	`slice="requirements"`, `<constraint name="pass">requirements</constraint>`)
141	records, from the requirements (`requirements.md` and the documents it
142	cites), the design when one binds, the product docs and the ledger, what the
143	requirements ASK: the problem against the code, which acceptance criteria are
144	ambiguous or untestable as written (or missing, when a prompt or a document
145	states behaviour as prose and no criterion yet), the
146	PRD feature the work belongs to, the risks in the requirements, the
147	candidate **contexts** the PRD features suggest, and the questions for the
148	user. Each impact lane (`phase="impact-analyst"` `slice="<area>"`) records what
149	code the requirements TOUCH in its area: the candidate impact surface
150	(components, files, tests, configuration) with a `path:line` citation for each
151	entry and the bounded context it belongs to, named in plain words, the
152	API-surface evidence, the code risks and the seams into other areas. The notes are what
153	the impact reviewer checks the draft against; a draft with no notes is a
154	blocking finding. No lane writes the draft.
155	
156	**The survey ends with `## Questions for the user`**, in four groups — the
157	whole of what Stage 2 takes to the user:
158	
159	- **(a) Open questions** the code and docs cannot answer — the answer changes
160	  the impact map, the acceptance criteria or the verdict. Each says what the
161	  analysis would proceed on if it stays unanswered, or that it blocks
162	  (every default could build the wrong thing).
163	- **(b) Conventional defaults** the analysis would assume — each phrased
164	  `Assumed: <default> — confirm or correct`.
165	- **(c) Proposed refined acceptance criteria** — the rewrite of each
166	  ambiguous, untestable or contradicted criterion, and each missing one.
167	- **(d) The feature**: a `features` correction when the PRD features the work touches
168	  differ from the requirements' `features`, and — when the run has no feature
169	  yet (`context.requirements.feature` null and no ticket `features`) — the
170	  PRD feature slugs it most likely belongs to, best first, or a new slug when
171	  none fits (slugs, `acs.py slug --text "<PRD feature name>"`; ADR-0120).
172	
173	Researchable facts are never questions: the survey reads the code, the docs,
174	the ledger and the previous analysis instead. An empty group says `_None._`.
175	
176	## A bug — reproduce first
177	
178	When the run's ticket is a `bug` (its `type` in the ticket file; ADR-0138), the
179	requirements lane reproduces it BEFORE it records anything else, because every
180	other entry — the problem, the criteria, the impact — rests on knowing what
181	actually happens:
182	
183	1. Read the bug's fields from the ticket: `reproduction` (the steps),
184	   `expected`, `actual`, `environment`, `severity`, and the suspected area its
185	   description names (a lead, never a finding).
186	2. Follow the steps against the checkout as it is, WITHOUT changing a repo file:
187	   run the existing test, CLI or endpoint the steps exercise; a scratch script,
188	   when one is needed, lives under `steps/analyze-requirements/` (written through
189	   `acs.py write`), never in the repo. Quote every command and its output.
190	3. Record the outcome in the notes under `## Reproduction`:
191	   - **reproduced** — the commands, the observed output matching `actual`, and
192	     the code path it runs through (`path:line`), which seeds the impact lanes'
193	     map and the regression test the plan writes first;
194	   - **not reproduced** — what was run and what happened instead, plus an
195	     **(a) open question** naming what is missing (an environment, data, a
196	     version, a step) and what the analysis proceeds on meanwhile. A bug that
197	     cannot be reproduced is never analyzed as if it had been.
198	
199	The draft carries the outcome in the README — the reproduction (or its
200	failure) in `## Scope and summary`, an unreproduced bug's question under
201	`## Questions and assumptions` — with no new heading: the README's six headings
202	are fixed. The criterion that a regression test reproduces the bug stays as the
203	ticket states it; refine its wording, never drop it.
204

# /acs:analyze-requirements — revising, reviewing and publishing the draft

Open this when a `draft` action carries `findings` (iteration ≥ 2), when the
`review` action is due, and when the `publish` action is due. The first
draft of a run needs only SKILL.md's Stage 3 and
`references/analysis-templates.md`.

**Where the cross-references below point.** "Two modes", "Stage 1",
"Stage 2" and "Stage 3" are SKILL.md's sections; "The feature" is
`references/clarify.md`.

## Revising the draft — iteration ≥ 2

On iteration ≥ 2 the action's `findings` are the previous iteration's
blocking findings, verbatim: put them ALL in the draft pass's `<context>`; it
fixes every one and nothing else in the seeded folder (deleting a context file
the analysis no longer has), recording them in `iter-<n>/authoring.md`.
A reviewer finding that is really a new question for the user — or a draft
pass that returns `needs_input` — goes through Stage 2 again (ledger first,
then one grouped ask) before the draft pass re-runs with the answers in
`<context>`: the controller blocks with `kind: "needs_input"` and hands you
`clarify` on the same iteration.

The working draft is a folder, `steps/analyze-requirements/iter-<n>/analysis/`
— the `draft` action prints it; when an iteration fails, the controller seeds
the next iteration's folder with a copy, so the draft is revised in place. The
published folder is a copy of those exact bytes (Publishing, below).

## The impact review

The `review` action. Spawn the three slices it prints (Judge slices, in
`references/fan-out.md`) in
ONE message, each with `<inputs>` of the draft folder (the action's `draft`,
and every file in its `draft_files`, README first), the authoring notes (the
action's `notes`), the analyst report (`analyst_report`), `requirements.md`
(its `## Refined` section as Stage 2 left it) and, on a ticket run, the ticket
file, the clarification ledger, `tech-design.md` when it binds, and the repo paths
the impact maps name. Each judges fresh — never forward the
analyst's reasoning — and judges EVERY file plus the README's contexts table:
the `surface` slice re-derives the impact map from the codebase itself (and
whether the contexts split it honestly) and checks that every `## Questions for the user` item was
answered in the ledger or carried as an open/assumed entry, and that the
confirmed criteria match the refined requirements (and the ticket). Each writes
`steps/analyze-requirements/iter-<n>/impact-reviewer-<slice>.md`. Then
`record-review`: the controller joins the reports into
`iter-<n>/impact-reviewer.md` and derives the verdict from the slices'
`<result>` snapshots plus the draft's deterministic checks (below) — never
conclude a pass yourself.

## The deterministic checks

**The deterministic checks run beside the review.** `record-draft` runs the
$0 folder checks on the draft as it records it (`acs_lib.analysis_folder`) —
the same front-matter specs and section lists the `form` slice re-runs — so
they are done before the review spawns, not after it passes; the `review`
action lists their findings as `draft_checks`. Per file, they are:

```bash
# README.md
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/front_matter_check.py" \
  --require "ticket: str; ready_for_planning: bool" \
  --ticket <id> "<draft>/README.md"
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/structure_lint.py" \
  --sections "Scope and summary; Contexts; Refined acceptance criteria; Cross-cutting risks and decisions; Questions and assumptions; Verdict" \
  --ordered "<draft>/README.md"

# every context file
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/front_matter_check.py" \
  --require "context: str" "<draft>/order-checkout.md"
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/structure_lint.py" \
  --sections "Impact map; Rules and edge cases; Risks; Open questions; API notes" \
  --ordered "<draft>/order-checkout.md"
```

and, across the folder: every file name is `README.md` or kebab-case `.md`
(no `index.md`, no subfolder), every `## Contexts` link resolves to a file in
the folder, every context file is linked, and `context` equals its file name.
(On a run with no ticket the README spec names `feature: str` in place of
`ticket: str` and takes no `--ticket`; a Discovery draft adds the version keys
to both specs, and `feature` to the context spec; `record-draft` picks the
specs from the run — you never choose them.)

`record-review` folds them into that iteration's blocking findings: a check
finding fails the iteration like a judge's blocking finding (it goes to the
next draft pass, or ends the run at the cap), never patched by you.

## Publishing

Once those pass, `publish` copies
every file of the draft folder byte-for-byte to the resolved analysis folder —
the feature's living analysis on a Discovery run,
`<development_dir>/<feature>/<ticket-id or run-id>/analysis/` on a shared
Development run, the run's state folder on a LOCAL one (recorded in
`publication`, never in `publication.files`) — removes a context file the new
analysis no longer has (only inside that folder), reads every file back, and
records the repo paths it wrote as `publication.files` in the loop,
repo-relative, with each file's sha. It never
stages, commits or pushes and refuses no branch (ADR-0127): the files are left
as uncommitted changes in the working tree, and `/acs:create-pr` reads those
recorded paths to make the documents commit, the first of the PR.
`record-publication` re-derives it from the working tree — every published
file is still the reviewed bytes — and completes the loop.

You never copy or commit the analysis yourself, and no subagent does: the
file-map write guard (`acs_lib/filemap.py`) denies any running `write`-kind
agent — the analyst included — a write under the run's document folders, because
these documents are precisely the control inputs an implementer is checked
against. The partition draft is workspace state and is never committed.

The front-matter check uses the same parser the gates and the analysis
folder check use, so a draft it accepts cannot be rejected downstream for its
front matter.

**The published file is the reusable record.** The run's
analysis folder is what `/acs:create-impl-plan`, `/acs:create-api-contract` and
`/acs:create-test-docs` read, and what the next run of this skill starts from
(Stage 1's reuse); the feature's living analysis is what the Design skills
(`/acs:create-architecture`, `/acs:create-data-design`, `/acs:create-flows`,
`/acs:create-tech-design`) read and what every later Development run on the feature
starts from. Every reader opens the README first (`artifacts["analysis.md"]`)
and then only the context files it needs (`analysis_files`). The partition
copy exists only for the no-checkout case, where there is no docs folder to
publish to.

the same front-matter specs and section lists the `form` slice re-runs — so
they are done before the review spawns, not after it passes; the `review`
action lists their findings as `draft_checks`. Per file, they are:

```bash
# README.md
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/front_matter_check.py" \
  --require "ticket: str; ready_for_planning: bool" \
  --ticket <id> "<draft>/README.md"
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/structure_lint.py" \
  --sections "Scope and summary; Contexts; Refined acceptance criteria; Cross-cutting risks and decisions; Questions and assumptions; Verdict" \
  --ordered "<draft>/README.md"

# every context file
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/front_matter_check.py" \
  --require "context: str" "<draft>/order-checkout.md"
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/structure_lint.py" \
  --sections "Impact map; Rules and edge cases; Risks; Open questions; API notes" \
  --ordered "<draft>/order-checkout.md"
```

and, across the folder: every file name is `README.md` or kebab-case `.md`
(no `index.md`, no subfolder), every `## Contexts` link resolves to a file in
the folder, every context file is linked, and `context` equals its file name.
(On a run with no ticket the README spec names `feature: str` in place of
`ticket: str` and takes no `--ticket`; a Discovery draft adds the version keys
to both specs, and `feature` to the context spec; `record-draft` picks the
specs from the run — you never choose them.)

`record-review` folds them into that iteration's blocking findings: a check
finding fails the iteration like a judge's blocking finding (it goes to the
next draft pass, or ends the run at the cap), never patched by you.

## Publishing

Once those pass, `publish` copies
every file of the draft folder byte-for-byte to the resolved analysis folder —
the feature's living analysis on a Discovery run,
`<development_dir>/<feature>/<ticket-id or run-id>/analysis/` on a shared
Development run, the run's state folder on a LOCAL one (recorded in
`publication`, never in `publication.files`) — removes a context file the new
analysis no longer has (only inside that folder), reads every file back, and
records the repo paths it wrote as `publication.files` in the loop,
repo-relative, with each file's sha. It never
stages, commits or pushes and refuses no branch (ADR-0127): the files are left
as uncommitted changes in the working tree, and `/acs:create-pr` reads those
recorded paths to make the documents commit, the first of the PR.
`record-publication` re-derives it from the working tree — every published
file is still the reviewed bytes — and completes the loop.

You never copy or commit the analysis yourself, and no subagent does: the
file-map write guard (`acs_lib/filemap.py`) denies any running `write`-kind
agent — the analyst included — a write under the run's document folders, because
these documents are precisely the control inputs an implementer is checked
against. The partition draft is workspace state and is never committed.

The front-matter check uses the same parser the gates and the analysis
folder check use, so a draft it accepts cannot be rejected downstream for its
front matter.

**The published file is the reusable record.** The run's
analysis folder is what `/acs:create-impl-plan`, `/acs:create-api-contract` and
`/acs:create-test-docs` read, and what the next run of this skill starts from
(Stage 1's reuse); the feature's living analysis is what the Design skills
(`/acs:create-architecture`, `/acs:create-data-design`, `/acs:create-flows`,
`/acs:create-tech-design`) read and what every later Development run on the feature
starts from. Every reader opens the README first (`artifacts["analysis.md"]`)
and then only the context files it needs (`analysis_files`). The partition
copy exists only for the no-checkout case, where there is no docs folder to
publish to.

2	
3	Read this before the analysis draft is written — the analyst in its `draft`
4	pass, and the coordinator when the `draft` action is due: the README's and
5	each context file's exact front matter and headings, what each section
6	carries, how the files are written, and the load-bearing surfaces the Risks
7	must name. The survey and the synthesis need none of it.
8	
9	## The folder
10	
11	The `draft` pass writes a folder for people first: plain-word headings, short
12	sections, a README someone can read without opening anything else. Every file
13	name is `README.md` or kebab-case `.md` made of plain words (no `index.md`, no
14	subfolder, nothing else). The analysis is read by machines as well as people:
15	the README's front matter (`ready_for_planning` above all, which
16	`/acs:create-impl-plan` reads) is part of the deliverable, not decoration. Emit
17	exactly these keys, with
18	these types, and exactly these headings in this order (the task's
19	`<constraint name="mode">` and `<constraint name="feature">` say which front
20	matter applies).
21	
22	The folder holds two kinds of file.
23	
24	## The README — `README.md`
25	
26	**The README** — `README.md`, readable on its own by someone who opens nothing
27	else: EXACTLY this front matter and these six headings, in this order:
28	
29	```markdown
30	---
31	ticket: SHOP-123
32	ready_for_planning: true
33	---
34	
35	# Analysis — SHOP-123: Accept CSV imports over 10 MB
36	
37	## Scope and summary
38	## Contexts
39	## Refined acceptance criteria
40	## Cross-cutting risks and decisions
41	## Questions and assumptions
42	## Verdict
43	```
44	
45	- **Front matter.** `ticket` is the ticket id; a run with no ticket writes
46	  `feature: <slug>` in its place. `ready_for_planning` is the
47	  verdict below, as a boolean. Never invent another key and never omit one of
48	  the two — except that a Discovery draft (`mode` discovery: the feature's
49	  living analysis) opens with the ADR-0122 version keys before them: `status:
50	  proposed`, `version` (the living analysis's `version` + 1, or `1` when there
51	  is none), `tickets` (carried over from the living analysis, `[]` when there
52	  is none) and `feature`. There is no `api_surface` key (ADR-0134) and no
53	  `needs_design_recommendation` (ADR-0139): an older analysis that still
54	  carries one is read with the key ignored, and none is written. The analysis
55	  never judges whether a design is needed.
56	- **`## Scope and summary`** — the requirements in terms of this repository,
57	  in a few sentences: the behaviour that changes, for whom, what "done"
58	  means, and what is out of scope. Name every disagreement between the
59	  requirements' prose and the code, each citing the file that contradicts it.
60	- **`## Contexts`** — a table, one row per context file, linked by its bare
61	  file name (no `/`, no anchor); every context file is listed, and only those
62	  — the controller refuses a link that does not resolve and a context file
63	  the table does not list:
64	
65	  | Context | File | Purpose |
66	  | --- | --- | --- |
67	  | CSV import | [csv-import.md](csv-import.md) | how an uploaded file becomes rows |
68	
69	- **`## Refined acceptance criteria`** — every criterion of the
70	  requirements, quoted with its `AC-n`, marked `testable` / `ambiguous` /
71	  `untestable` / `contradicted` / `missing`, with the rewrite for each
72	  non-clean entry and its state: `confirmed (C-n)` when the user confirmed it
73	  and the coordinator recorded it (`requirements refine`, which also amends
74	  the ticket when there is one) — quote it as `requirements.md`'s
75	  `## Refined` now carries it; `rejected (C-n)`; or `proposed — open (C-n)`
76	  when unanswered. Never present an unconfirmed
77	  rewrite as applied. Name the context file(s) each criterion lands in.
78	- **`## Cross-cutting risks and decisions`** — only what spans contexts or
79	  the whole change: the interfaces it adds or alters (each named, or "none" —
80	  an interface change is designed with `/acs:create-api-contract`) with
81	  their reason, a risk two contexts share, a load-bearing surface (each linked to the context
82	  file that details it). One-context risks stay in that context file.
83	- **`## Questions and assumptions`** — one line per clarification entry, by
84	  its `C-n` id and status (`open`, `answered`, `assumed`), with the question
85	  and the answer, or the rationale when assumed. Every item of the notes'
86	  `## Questions for the user` appears here as its `C-n`; the ledger
87	  (`clarifications.json`) is the source of truth. Then the assumptions: only
88	  what the user did not answer, with why each is needed and what breaks if it
89	  is wrong (a ledger entry with `--source assumption` included). A default
90	  the user confirmed is an answer, not an assumption. `_None recorded._` when
91	  there are none.
92	- **`## Verdict`** — `ready_for_planning: true` or `false`, in prose, with the
93	  reason. `false` requires naming exactly what is missing and which open
94	  question would settle it — and the question must be one where every
95	  default could build the wrong thing (a contradiction with the code, a
96	  design document or an ADR; a behaviour the criteria depend on that nothing
97	  defines; a fork in scope). A detail with a conventional default — "prints"
98	  means stdout, a credential check is exact and case-sensitive, argument
99	  counts the requirements never mention are out of scope — is never a reason for
100	  `false`: the user confirmed or corrected it, or, unanswered, it is an
101	  assumption recorded in `## Questions and assumptions` with a proposed
102	  criterion rewrite.
103	
104	## One file per context — `<context>.md`
105	
106	**One file per context** — `<context>.md`, one per context of the notes'
107	`## Contexts`, named by its file name there: a kebab-case name made of plain
108	words (never `index.md`, no subfolder), with EXACTLY this front matter and
109	these five headings, in this order:
110	
111	```markdown
112	---
113	context: csv-import
114	---
115	
116	# CSV import
117	
118	## Impact map
119	## Rules and edge cases
120	## Risks
121	## Open questions
122	## API notes
123	```
124	
125	- **Front matter.** `context` is the file name without `.md`. A Discovery
126	  draft adds, after `context`, `feature`, `status: proposed`, `version` and
127	  `tickets` — the same values as the README.
128	- **`## Impact map`** — a table, and its FIRST column is a repo-relative path,
129	  because that column is how a reader sees what this change actually touches:
130	
131	  | Path | Component | Change | Evidence |
132	  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
133	  | `src/import/api.py` | import API | new size branch on upload | `api.py:88` rejects >10 MB today |
134	  | `tests/test_import_api.py` | import API tests | new cases for the large-file path | covers `upload()` at `:41` |
135	
136	  Source, tests, docs and configuration all belong here. Every row carries
137	  evidence you read. A file the change CREATES is a row too, marked as new.
138	- **`## Rules and edge cases`** — the business rules this context enforces
139	  that the change touches, and the edge cases a test must cover, each cited.
140	- **`## Risks`** — implementation and shipping risks in this context with
141	  their evidence and, where one exists, the mitigation the implementation
142	  plan should consider; a load-bearing surface named with its paths.
143	- **`## Open questions`** — the `C-n` entries that concern this context only,
144	  by id and status (the README holds the full list), or `_None._`.
145	- **`## API notes`** — the surface this context adds or changes (endpoint,
146	  flag, message, schema), cited, or `_None._`.
147	
148	A context file never restates another's rows, rules or risks: it links to the
149	file that owns them (`see [payment-refunds.md](payment-refunds.md)`).
150	
151	## Without a ticket, and on a Discovery run
152	
153	On a run with no ticket the README's first key is `feature: <slug>` in place of `ticket:`, and its title
154	reads `# Analysis — <feature>: <subject>`. A Discovery run's draft — the
155	feature's living analysis — opens the README with the version keys of
156	ADR-0122 before the three above: `status: proposed`, `version` (the living
157	analysis's `version` + 1, or `1` for the feature's first analysis), `tickets`
158	(carried over from the living analysis) and `feature`; each context file then
159	carries `feature` and the same three version keys after `context`:
160	
161	```yaml
162	---
163	status: proposed
164	version: 2
165	tickets: ["SHOP-120"]
166	feature: wishlist
167	ready_for_planning: true
168	---
169	```
170	
171	## What the review holds the draft to
172	
173	This skill is where the requirements' ambiguities are SUPPOSED to surface, so the
174	README's `## Questions and assumptions` and the ledger are the same set of
175	facts in two places: every question is a ledger entry, and that section names
176	each entry by its `C-n` id and its status, so the next skill can see what is
177	still open. A question that concerns one context only is also listed in that
178	context file's `## Open questions`, by the same `C-n`.
179	
180	What each section carries is defined above; the
181	contract that matters here is that every context file's `## Impact map` is a
182	table whose first column is a repo-relative path (that column is what the
183	load-bearing-surface step below reads), that the README's front-matter values
184	agree with the sections beneath them, and that the answers show: the README's
185	`## Questions and assumptions` lists every `C-n` with its answer or status and
186	holds as assumptions only what the user did not answer, and
187	`## Refined acceptance criteria` states which criteria were confirmed into the
188	requirements (and so the ticket, when there is one). Keep every section short;
189	an empty one says `_None._`. The README summarizes and links — it never
190	copies a context file's rows.
191	
192	## Writing the files
193	
194	The analyst writes and revises every file through Bash with acs's own
195	writer — `python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/acs.py" write <path>
196	<<'ACS_EOF'`, the file's content, then `ACS_EOF` alone on the last line; an
197	in-place revision reads the file and writes it whole again the same way —
198	never through the Write or Edit tool. The draft lives in acs's workspace,
199	in the main checkout (ADR-0136), where a session in a worktree is refused
200	any Write/Edit; and the runtime also refuses a subagent's Write/Edit of a
201	file named like a report ("Subagents should return findings as text, not
202	write report files"), so each attempt would be a turn lost before the same
203	content lands via Bash anyway.
204	
205	## Load-bearing surfaces — name them in the context's `## Risks`
206	
207	The impact map is the first place anyone can see WHAT this change touches, and
208	that is the single strongest input to the delivery-path judgement /acs:ship
209	makes later from the plan (ADR-0095). Nothing here writes a rigor setting —
210	there is no `stakes` axis any more, and this skill does not classify — but the
211	analysis is where the evidence for that judgement is recorded.
212	
213	So when the impact map reaches a surface the repo treats as load-bearing —
214	authentication or authorization, payments, a migration or any stored shape, a
215	public API other systems call, concurrency or ordering, anything the repo's own
216	architecture docs flag — say so explicitly in that context file's `## Risks`, naming the paths, and
217	list it again, linked, under the README's `## Cross-cutting risks and
218	decisions`. A
219	risk entry that names a boundary is read by `/acs:create-impl-plan` (which
220	carries it into the plan's own Risks section) and then by whoever judges the
221	path, and it is what turns a one-file change into a `standard` or `complex`
222	run instead of a `trivial` one.
223	
224	Prose, not a setting: what makes this work is that the risk is stated where a
225	reader will weigh it, not that a glob matched.

# Analysis — EVAL-1: Cursor pagination for GET /customers

## Scope and summary

Clients that page `GET /customers` by offset skip or repeat customers when rows are inserted between requests. The change adds an opaque `cursor` query parameter, a `next_cursor` field on every response (null on the last page), and a 400 `invalid_cursor` rejection for a malformed cursor. Done means AC-1..AC-3 hold and the README API line documents the new behaviour. Offset paging stays, deprecated, and the cursor wins when both are given (C-2). The limit defaults to 20 with a maximum of 250 (C-3). Out of scope: a customer data store, and any change to the PRD.

Disagreements between the requirements and the code:
- The ticket says "Replace" offset, but C-2 keeps it (deprecated). The recorded answer governs.
- The PRD marks Customer listing as shipped (`docs/product/prd.md:21`), but `list_customers` is a stub returning `"items": []` (`src/shop/__init__.py:8-9`). No store, customer id or HTTP layer exists. The cursor encodes the last customer id (C-1) and nothing in the code defines ids.
- C-3 sets a maximum limit of 250, but `limit` is unbounded today (`src/shop/__init__.py:8`).
- The living analysis cites README.md:7 for the `/customers` line. It is now README.md:8 (`:7` is `/health`).

## Contexts

| Context | File | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer listing | [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md) | how a client pages through customers: cursor, next_cursor, offset, limit, invalid_cursor |

## Refined acceptance criteria

No refinements. The user was unreachable and the criteria stand as written. All land in [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md).
- **AC-1** "GET /customers accepts an optional cursor query parameter and returns the page of customers that follows it" - testable. "Follows" means customers after the id the cursor encodes (C-1).
- **AC-2** "Every GET /customers response carries next_cursor, which is null on the last page" - testable. It applies to offset-mode responses too (C-5).
- **AC-3** "A malformed cursor is rejected with HTTP 400 and error code invalid_cursor" - testable (C-4).

## Cross-cutting risks and decisions

- Interface altered: `GET /customers` gains the `cursor` parameter, a `next_cursor` response field and a 400 `invalid_cursor` error. Design it with `/acs:create-api-contract` before planning the implementation.
- Load-bearing surface: the public API `GET /customers`, documented at `README.md:8` and called by clients, with its response shape at `src/shop/__init__.py:9`. It also involves ordering: exactly-once walking depends on a stable, monotonic id order. Details in [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md#risks).
- No transport layer exists in the repo, so where the HTTP 400 is produced is undecided. Tests can judge only function-level behaviour until it exists. See [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md#risks).

## Questions and assumptions

- C-1 answered: cursor is the URL-safe base64 of the last customer id, opaque.
- C-2 answered: offset stays, deprecated; the cursor wins when both are given.
- C-3 answered: limit default 20, max 250.
- C-4 answered: a malformed cursor returns HTTP 400 with code `invalid_cursor`.
- C-5 assumed: `next_cursor` is present (null on the last page) in offset-mode responses too, from AC-2 "every response". If wrong, AC-2 would need narrowing to cursor mode.
- C-6 assumed: the 250 maximum applies to `limit` in both modes. If wrong, offset callers could still request unbounded pages.

## Verdict

`ready_for_planning: true`. Every question is answered or carries a conventional default, and the criteria are testable as written. The missing store, ids and HTTP layer are risks for the plan, not open questions: the ticket and C-4 fix the observable behaviour. Run `/acs:create-api-contract` for the `GET /customers` change.
ACS_EOF

---
context: customer-listing
---

# Customer listing

## Impact map

| Path | Component | Change | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/shop/__init__.py` | `list_customers(offset=0, limit=PAGE_SIZE)`, `PAGE_SIZE = 20` | accept optional `cursor`; return `next_cursor` (null on last page) in every response; reject a malformed cursor as `invalid_cursor` (400); cursor wins over offset; cap `limit` at 250 | `:8-9` function and `{"items","offset","limit"}` return; `:1` PAGE_SIZE |
| `tests/test_customer_listing.py` | listing tests (new) | new cases for AC-1..AC-3, precedence, limit bounds | no test covers `list_customers`; `tests/test_health.py:1-5` is the sibling; `pyproject.toml:5-6` pytest `pythonpath` is `src` |
| `README.md` | API docs | document `cursor`, `next_cursor`, the 400 `invalid_cursor`, offset deprecation, limit max | `README.md:8` `GET /customers?offset=&limit=` |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | release notes | new entry for the change | `CHANGELOG.md:3-5` holds only the 2.4.0 "Customer listing." entry |

## Rules and edge cases

- Cursor is the URL-safe base64 of the last customer id, opaque to clients (C-1).
- Both `offset` and `cursor` given: the cursor wins (C-2). A malformed cursor with offset present still returns 400 (AC-3 with C-4).
- `limit` defaults to 20 and is capped at 250 in both modes (C-3, C-6).
- `next_cursor` is always present and null on the last page, including offset-mode responses (AC-2, C-5).
- Test cases: last page, an empty result, a cursor naming the last id, a non-base64 cursor, a base64 cursor that is not a valid id, `limit` of 250 and 251, and a customer inserted between pages (not repeated or skipped).

## Risks

- Load-bearing public API: `GET /customers` (`README.md:8`, `src/shop/__init__.py:8-9`) is called by clients. Adding `next_cursor` is additive, but offset and limit behaviour must stay compatible (C-2). The existing `offset` response key's fate in cursor mode is a plan detail.
- Ordering: exactly-once walking relies on ordering by a monotonic customer id (C-1). No code defines customers or ids (`src/shop/__init__.py:9` returns a stub), so the plan must settle the ordering source.
- No transport layer: the repo holds only `src/shop/__init__.py` under `src`, so the HTTP 400 mapping has no home. Tests will judge the function's return or raise behaviour, not an HTTP status. Mitigation: the plan decides where the error is mapped.
- No existing coverage of `list_customers`; the new test file is the only judge.
- Limit cap at 250 is new behaviour for current offset callers who pass larger limits (`src/shop/__init__.py:8` is unbounded).

## Open questions

_None._ C-1..C-4 answered; C-5 and C-6 assumed (see the README).

## API notes

`GET /customers` (`README.md:8`): adds the optional `cursor` query parameter; every response gains `next_cursor` (string, or null on the last page); a malformed cursor returns HTTP 400 with error code `invalid_cursor`; `offset` is kept but deprecated; `limit` defaults to 20 and is at most 250. The carrying symbol is `list_customers` (`src/shop/__init__.py:8`). Design the contract with `/acs:create-api-contract`.

}

# Analysis — EVAL-1: Cursor pagination for GET /customers

## Scope and summary

Clients that page `GET /customers` by offset skip or repeat customers when rows are inserted between requests. The change adds an opaque `cursor` query parameter, a `next_cursor` field on every response (null on the last page), and a 400 `invalid_cursor` rejection for a malformed cursor. Done means AC-1..AC-3 hold and the README API line documents the new behaviour. Offset paging stays, deprecated, and the cursor wins when both are given (C-2). The limit defaults to 20 with a maximum of 250 (C-3). Out of scope: a customer data store, and any change to the PRD.

Disagreements between the requirements and the code:
- The ticket says "Replace" offset, but C-2 keeps it (deprecated). The recorded answer governs.
- The PRD marks Customer listing as shipped (`docs/product/prd.md:21`), but `list_customers` is a stub returning `"items": []` (`src/shop/__init__.py:8-9`). No store, customer id or HTTP layer exists. The cursor encodes the last customer id (C-1) and nothing in the code defines ids.
- C-3 sets a maximum limit of 250, but `limit` is unbounded today (`src/shop/__init__.py:8`).
- The living analysis cites README.md:7 for the `/customers` line. It is now README.md:8 (`:7` is `/health`).

## Contexts

| Context | File | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer listing | [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md) | how a client pages through customers: cursor, next_cursor, offset, limit, invalid_cursor |

## Refined acceptance criteria

No refinements. The user was unreachable and the criteria stand as written. All land in [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md).
- **AC-1** "GET /customers accepts an optional cursor query parameter and returns the page of customers that follows it" - testable. "Follows" means customers after the id the cursor encodes (C-1).
- **AC-2** "Every GET /customers response carries next_cursor, which is null on the last page" - testable. It applies to offset-mode responses too (C-5).
- **AC-3** "A malformed cursor is rejected with HTTP 400 and error code invalid_cursor" - testable (C-4).

## Cross-cutting risks and decisions

- Interface altered: `GET /customers` gains the `cursor` parameter, a `next_cursor` response field and a 400 `invalid_cursor` error. Design it with `/acs:create-api-contract` before planning the implementation.
- Load-bearing surface: the public API `GET /customers`, documented at `README.md:8` and called by clients, with its response shape at `src/shop/__init__.py:9`. It also involves ordering: exactly-once walking depends on a stable, monotonic id order. Details in [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md#risks).
- No transport layer exists in the repo, so where the HTTP 400 is produced is undecided. Tests can judge only function-level behaviour until it exists. See [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md#risks).

## Questions and assumptions

- C-1 answered: cursor is the URL-safe base64 of the last customer id, opaque.
- C-2 answered: offset stays, deprecated; the cursor wins when both are given.
- C-3 answered: limit default 20, max 250.
- C-4 answered: a malformed cursor returns HTTP 400 with code `invalid_cursor`.
- C-5 assumed: `next_cursor` is present (null on the last page) in offset-mode responses too, from AC-2 "every response". If wrong, AC-2 would need narrowing to cursor mode.
- C-6 assumed: the 250 maximum applies to `limit` in both modes. If wrong, offset callers could still request unbounded pages.

## Verdict

`ready_for_planning: true`. Every question is answered or carries a conventional default, and the criteria are testable as written. The missing store, ids and HTTP layer are risks for the plan, not open questions: the ticket and C-4 fix the observable behaviour. Run `/acs:create-api-contract` for the `GET /customers` change.

# Analysis — EVAL-1: Cursor pagination for GET /customers

## Scope and summary

Clients that page `GET /customers` by offset skip or repeat customers when rows are inserted between requests. The change adds an opaque `cursor` query parameter, a `next_cursor` field on every response (null on the last page), and a 400 `invalid_cursor` rejection for a malformed cursor. Done means AC-1..AC-3 hold and the README API line documents the new behaviour. Offset paging stays, deprecated, and the cursor wins when both are given (C-2). The limit defaults to 20 with a maximum of 250 (C-3). Out of scope: a customer data store, and any change to the PRD.

Disagreements between the requirements and the code:
- The ticket says "Replace" offset, but C-2 keeps it (deprecated). The recorded answer governs.
- The PRD marks Customer listing as shipped (`docs/product/prd.md:21`), but `list_customers` is a stub returning `"items": []` (`src/shop/__init__.py:8-9`). No store, customer id or HTTP layer exists. The cursor encodes the last customer id (C-1) and nothing in the code defines ids.
- C-3 sets a maximum limit of 250, but `limit` is unbounded today (`src/shop/__init__.py:8`).
- The living analysis cites README.md:7 for the `/customers` line. It is now README.md:8 (`:7` is `/health`).

## Contexts

| Context | File | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer listing | [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md) | how a client pages through customers: cursor, next_cursor, offset, limit, invalid_cursor |

## Refined acceptance criteria

No refinements. The user was unreachable and the criteria stand as written. All land in [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md).
- **AC-1** "GET /customers accepts an optional cursor query parameter and returns the page of customers that follows it" - testable. "Follows" means customers after the id the cursor encodes (C-1).
- **AC-2** "Every GET /customers response carries next_cursor, which is null on the last page" - testable. It applies to offset-mode responses too (C-5).
- **AC-3** "A malformed cursor is rejected with HTTP 400 and error code invalid_cursor" - testable (C-4).

## Cross-cutting risks and decisions

- Interface altered: `GET /customers` gains the `cursor` parameter, a `next_cursor` response field and a 400 `invalid_cursor` error. Design it with `/acs:create-api-contract` before planning the implementation.
- Load-bearing surface: the public API `GET /customers`, documented at `README.md:8` and called by clients, with its response shape at `src/shop/__init__.py:9`. It also involves ordering: exactly-once walking depends on a stable, monotonic id order. Details in [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md#risks).
- No transport layer exists in the repo, so where the HTTP 400 is produced is undecided. Tests can judge only function-level behaviour until it exists. See [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md#risks).

## Questions and assumptions

- C-1 answered: cursor is the URL-safe base64 of the last customer id, opaque.
- C-2 answered: offset stays, deprecated; the cursor wins when both are given.
- C-3 answered: limit default 20, max 250.
- C-4 answered: a malformed cursor returns HTTP 400 with code `invalid_cursor`.
- C-5 assumed: `next_cursor` is present (null on the last page) in offset-mode responses too, from AC-2 "every response". If wrong, AC-2 would need narrowing to cursor mode.
- C-6 assumed: the 250 maximum applies to `limit` in both modes. If wrong, offset callers could still request unbounded pages.

## Verdict

`ready_for_planning: true`. Every question is answered or carries a conventional default, and the criteria are testable as written. The missing store, ids and HTTP layer are risks for the plan, not open questions: the ticket and C-4 fix the observable behaviour. Run `/acs:create-api-contract` for the `GET /customers` change.

# Customer listing

## Impact map

| Path | Component | Change | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `src/shop/__init__.py` | `list_customers(offset=0, limit=PAGE_SIZE)`, `PAGE_SIZE = 20` | accept optional `cursor`; return `next_cursor` (null on last page) in every response; reject a malformed cursor as `invalid_cursor` (400); cursor wins over offset; cap `limit` at 250 | `:8-9` function and `{"items","offset","limit"}` return; `:1` PAGE_SIZE |
| `tests/test_customer_listing.py` | listing tests (new) | new cases for AC-1..AC-3, precedence, limit bounds | no test covers `list_customers`; `tests/test_health.py:1-5` is the sibling; `pyproject.toml:5-6` pytest `pythonpath` is `src` |
| `README.md` | API docs | document `cursor`, `next_cursor`, the 400 `invalid_cursor`, offset deprecation, limit max | `README.md:8` `GET /customers?offset=&limit=` |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | release notes | new entry for the change | `CHANGELOG.md:3-5` holds only the 2.4.0 "Customer listing." entry |

## Rules and edge cases

- Cursor is the URL-safe base64 of the last customer id, opaque to clients (C-1).
- Both `offset` and `cursor` given: the cursor wins (C-2). A malformed cursor with offset present still returns 400 (AC-3 with C-4).
- `limit` defaults to 20 and is capped at 250 in both modes (C-3, C-6).
- `next_cursor` is always present and null on the last page, including offset-mode responses (AC-2, C-5).
- Test cases: last page, an empty result, a cursor naming the last id, a non-base64 cursor, a base64 cursor that is not a valid id, `limit` of 250 and 251, and a customer inserted between pages (not repeated or skipped).

## Risks

- Load-bearing public API: `GET /customers` (`README.md:8`, `src/shop/__init__.py:8-9`) is called by clients. Adding `next_cursor` is additive, but offset and limit behaviour must stay compatible (C-2). The existing `offset` response key's fate in cursor mode is a plan detail.
- Ordering: exactly-once walking relies on ordering by a monotonic customer id (C-1). No code defines customers or ids (`src/shop/__init__.py:9` returns a stub), so the plan must settle the ordering source.
- No transport layer: the repo holds only `src/shop/__init__.py` under `src`, so the HTTP 400 mapping has no home. Tests will judge the function's return or raise behaviour, not an HTTP status. Mitigation: the plan decides where the error is mapped.
- No existing coverage of `list_customers`; the new test file is the only judge.
- Limit cap at 250 is new behaviour for current offset callers who pass larger limits (`src/shop/__init__.py:8` is unbounded).

## Open questions

_None._ C-1..C-4 answered; C-5 and C-6 assumed (see the README).

## API notes

`GET /customers` (`README.md:8`): adds the optional `cursor` query parameter; every response gains `next_cursor` (string, or null on the last page); a malformed cursor returns HTTP 400 with error code `invalid_cursor`; `offset` is kept but deprecated; `limit` defaults to 20 and is at most 250. The carrying symbol is `list_customers` (`src/shop/__init__.py:8`). Design the contract with `/acs:create-api-contract`.

Clients that page `GET /customers` by offset skip or repeat customers when rows are inserted between requests. Done means AC-1..AC-3 hold and the README API line documents the new behaviour. Offset paging stays, deprecated, and the cursor wins when both are given (C-2). The limit defaults to 20 with a maximum of 250 (C-3). Out of scope: a customer data store, and any change to the PRD.

- The ticket says "Replace" offset, but C-2 keeps it (deprecated). The recorded answer governs.

- C-3 sets a maximum limit of 250, but `limit` is unbounded today (`src/shop/__init__.py:8`).
- The living analysis cites README.md:7 for the `/customers` line. It is now README.md:8 (`:7` is `/health`).

# /acs:analyze-requirements — the result document and the report

Read this at Finish: before you write `steps/analyze-requirements/result.json`
(the example is SKILL.md's), what each canonical `states` key means and
must equal, and what a failed run keeps; before you report a direct
invocation, what its summary covers.

## The `states` keys

Canonical `states` keys — EXACT names; `acs step finish` documents
them and the next steps read them:
- `ready_for_planning` (bool): the verdict. `false` is the `needs_input`
  arm, and `/acs:create-impl-plan` is what consumes it. It MUST equal the
  published front matter's `ready_for_planning` (the README's) — a result
  document that disagrees with it is a defect, not a second opinion. There is
  no `api_surface` key any more (ADR-0134): an interface change is named in
  the README and pointed to `/acs:create-api-contract`.
- `questions_open` (int): clarifications still unanswered in the ledger —
  the count `clarify.py list --open` (`--ticket <id>` on a ticket run)
  prints after this run.
- `files` (array): every repo-relative path this run wrote and left
  uncommitted — the publish action's `publication.files` (every file of
  the published analysis folder, README first: the feature's living
  analysis on a Discovery run, e.g.
  `docs/product/features/wishlist/analysis/README.md`). `/acs:create-pr` commits
  them; empty when nothing was published or the analysis was kept local.

Confirmed criteria and features are applied through their own CLI
(`acs.py requirements refine`), so they belong in
`findings` and the completion report, not in `states`. On failure keep
whatever is true: `ready_for_planning: false`, the open findings in
`findings`, and the reason (`stalled`, the iteration cap, needs input) in
`summary` — the `failed` action's `stop_reason` and `reason`, verbatim.

## The direct-invocation summary

- Direct invocation: a compact summary — the verdict, the contexts it
  split the analysis into, the impact maps' component/file/test counts, what changed since the previous analysis
  when there was one, the interfaces it changes (and, when any, "an interface
  changes — design it with /acs:create-api-contract"), the questions asked
  and answered (or "Stage 2 skipped"), the feature it is filed under, the
  criteria and features confirmed into the requirements (and the
  ticket), any proposal still awaiting the user, open questions, where the
  analysis went ("shared to docs/development/…", "kept local (team
  default)", "kept local (this run only)"), the uncommitted files it left in
  the working tree, and the next step — on a
  Development run `/acs:create-impl-plan <id>` (`/acs:create-pr <id>` later
  commits everything the Development steps wrote); on a Discovery run the
  Design skills that read the feature's analysis (`/acs:create-tech-design`,
  `/acs:create-data-design <feature>`, `/acs:create-flows <feature>`) or
  `/acs:create-ticket` to turn it into delivery work.

# Analysis — EVAL-1: Cursor pagination for GET /customers

## Scope and summary

Clients that page `GET /customers` by offset skip or repeat customers when rows are inserted between requests. The change adds an opaque `cursor` query parameter, a `next_cursor` field on every response (null on the last page), and a 400 `invalid_cursor` rejection for a malformed cursor. Done means AC-1..AC-3 hold and the README API line documents the new behaviour. Offset paging stays, deprecated, and the cursor wins when both are given (C-2). The limit defaults to 20 with a maximum of 250 (C-3). Out of scope: a customer data store, and any change to the PRD.

Disagreements between the requirements and the code:
- The ticket says "Replace" offset, but C-2 keeps it (deprecated). The recorded answer governs.
- The PRD marks Customer listing as shipped (`docs/product/prd.md:21`), but `list_customers` is a stub returning `"items": []` (`src/shop/__init__.py:8-9`). No store, customer id or HTTP layer exists. The cursor encodes the last customer id (C-1) and nothing in the code defines ids.
- C-3 sets a maximum limit of 250, but `limit` is unbounded today (`src/shop/__init__.py:8`).
- The living analysis cites README.md:7 for the `/customers` line. It is now README.md:8 (`:7` is `/health`).

## Contexts

| Context | File | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer listing | [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md) | how a client pages through customers: cursor, next_cursor, offset, limit, invalid_cursor |

## Refined acceptance criteria

No refinements. The user was unreachable and the criteria stand as written. All land in [customer-listing.md](customer-listing.md).
- **AC-1** "GET /customers accepts an optional cursor query parameter and returns the page of customers that follows it" - testable. "Follows" means customers after the id the cursor encodes (C-1).
- **AC-2** "Every GET /customers response carries next_cursor, which is null on the last page" - testable. It applies to offset-mode responses too (C-5).
- **AC-3** "A malformed cursor is rejected with HTTP 400 and error code invalid_cursor" - testable (C-4).

- **Metrics**: iterations 1/3.
- **Next**: `/acs:create-api-contract EVAL-1`, then `/acs:create-impl-plan EVAL-1`. `/acs:create-pr EVAL-1` commits the files later.
